source.title: SafeDecoding: Defending against Jailbreak Attacks via Safety-Aware Decoding
source.authors: Zhangchen Xu; Feng-Qing Jiang; Luyao Niu; Jinyuan Jia; Bill Yuchen Lin; R. Poovendran

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some tables are flattened in the text, but the Table 1 ASR values used below can be assigned to the models, attacks, and defenses from the table layout.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates jailbreak success rates and a decoding intervention on aligned chat models, using its own attack and defense setup rather than the original studies’ methods or measures.
record.gate_note: The paper fine-tunes an expert model on up to 72 query/refusal pairs derived from 36 harmful queries; this is safety fine-tuning, not fine-tuning on harmful-compliance examples or benign instruction data. Its discussion of beginning a response with positive affirmation cites prior work; it does not test compliant prefilling. It does test jailbreak attacks and reports ASR, including under SafeDecoding. The top-p ablation reports a textual trend but no exact ASR values. The MT-bench and Just-Eval scores assess benign-task utility, not the claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is a defense paper. It builds SafeDecoding on the prior observation that attacks work by making the model open with an affirmative reply (Zou et al.). It therefore applies an expert-guided decoding change only to the first m=2 tokens, and it reports mainly its own defense's ASR against six baselines. The no-defense ASRs re-run standard published attacks as baselines. Most of these attacks are prompt-level jailbreaks (AutoDAN, PAIR, DeepInception, SAP30, Template), not opening, prefill or suffix manipulations. The paper never isolates whether bypass works through the response opening. It does not measure per-token KL, safety-relevant parameters, why safety is shallow, or fine-tuning effects on harmful compliance. Its fine-tuning is safety fine-tuning of an expert on at most 72 refusal pairs. The record's V4 'tests' reading over-reaches: the rows are baselines and own-method results, not a test of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that SafeDecoding, which amplifies safety-disclaimer tokens using a safety-fine-tuned expert during the first m decoding steps, substantially reduces jailbreak ASR and harmfulness across five models. They also conclude it preserves utility with small overhead and outperforms six baseline defenses.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a safety-focused LoRA expert from refusal examples and combines its token probabilities with the original model during decoding; it does not reproduce harmful-example fine-tuning or measure aligned-versus-base token KL.
record.method_sensitivity: In the SafeDecoding ablation, the authors report that ASR rises as top-p p increases. They also report that ASR and harmful scores decrease as m increases, with metrics stabilizing beyond a point; exact plotted values are not stated.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering only the first m=2 decoding steps toward an expert refusal model cuts ASR to 0–9% on Vicuna and about 0–4% on Llama2. In the m ablation, metrics stabilise for m≥2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Controlling the first few response tokens at inference is enough to restore refusal under most jailbreaks (the converse of V4).

fits_no_version.finding: In 31 of 250 responses, the model first rejects a harmful query and then complies with it under SafeDecoding.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A refusal opening does not guarantee a refusal; safety can fail after the first tokens.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2024 Main Conference)
record.problems: ASR uses keyword-based refusal-string detection, so it may not capture every refusal or compliance response. The paper gives no uncertainty intervals for the reported ASRs. It also reports a failure case and states that in 31 out of 250 responses the model may first reject a harmful query and then agree with it.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 harmful-score values and harmful-benchmark ASRs were not extracted because the selected rows focus on the version’s direct compliance-rate measure. Appendix B.1 Table 6 results for Guanaco, Falcon, and Dolphin were omitted because the text’s flattened table layout makes some model/condition assignments ambiguous. Table 7 expert-model results were also omitted.

untested.parts: No benign-data fine-tuning with a safety evaluation.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No compliant-prefill test, no isolation of opening tokens as the bypass route, and no decoding-change attacks on undefended models. Attack ASRs serve only as defense baselines.
LoRA is used only as a tool; parameter localization of safety is not tested.
No analysis of the data or objective causing shallowness.
No training that spreads safety deeper. SafeDecoding is an inference-time intervention on the first tokens.

missing.what: Ablation over m (number of SafeDecoding steps): ASR and harmful score fall as m rises and stabilise at m≥2. Figure-only values.
missing.versions: none (bears on first-token concentration only indirectly)

missing.what: Limitation: in 31 of 250 responses the model initially refuses, then complies.
The expert model fine-tuned on at most 72 refusal pairs still shows 8% GCG and 18% PAIR ASR on Vicuna, and MT-Bench falls to 3.46.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 labels are dropped. The 'supports' label rested on prompt-level jailbreaks (AutoDAN, PAIR, DeepInception, SAP30, Template) that do not manipulate the response opening. The 'limits_scope' labels rested on the study's own defense results, which are not evidence about the claim. The only opening-adjacent attack is GCG (a suffix), with no-defense ASR of 100% on Vicuna and 32% on Llama2-7b-chat; these are re-run baselines. ASR uses a keyword refusal judge. The study's design premise, that the first two tokens largely decide refusal, is consistent with shallow alignment but is assumed from Zou et al., not tested.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not fine-tune on examples that demonstrate harmful compliance or test whether such fine-tuning removes refusal.
No ordinary or carefully chosen benign-data fine-tuning is tested for its effect on harmful compliance.
The paper does not measure per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.

The paper tests six jailbreak attack methods and top-p sampling while SafeDecoding is active. It does not test compliant-token prefilling or compare a broad range of decoding changes on the undefended models.
LoRA is used to train an expert model, but the paper does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
The study does not test whether data or a training objective causes safety to be shallow in the first response tokens.
SafeDecoding is applied for a chosen number of initial tokens, but the study does not train safety to spread beyond the first tokens or test whether such training holds up.
